edits.old:
\begin{abstract}
As components of the electrical grid become increasingly connected through the internet, they face a growing threat from cyber attacks. This project developed a deep learning framework to detect anomalies in a multi-motor electrical motor testbed using features gathered by an electric measurement unit (EMU). EMUs are plug-and-play sensor devices placed at the Point of Common Coupling (PCC) that feed electrical motors in the testbed. EMUs provide voltage and current features at approximately 7~Hz with IoT compatibility and prototype hardware costing approximately US\$100 per unit. While initial baselines utilized standard Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, we ultimately developed a robust framework based on a multihead convolutional neural network (CNN) and bidirectional gated recurrent unit (Bi-GRU) architecture to better capture complex irregularities in time-series data. By addressing severe class imbalance and preserving raw signal context alongside temporal velocities, the rebalanced CNN--Bi-GRU model achieves 93.46\% accuracy and 95.32\% attack recall on 23,540 validation windows. Correct detection plus motor identification reaches 95.28\% in 596 configurations represented for both attacked motors while both motors operate. These are random overlapping-window validation results, not an independent-recording test.
edits.new:
\begin{abstract}
False data injection attacks (FDIAs) on motor-current feedback can disturb grid-edge loads while remaining difficult to identify from aggregate measurements. A low-cost detection framework is developed using an IoT-enabled electric measurement unit (EMU) at the point of common coupling (PCC). Plug-and-play EMUs can be deployed in large numbers, with voltage/current feature reporting supported up to 60~Hz. A two-motor testbed is operated at different speeds and loads, and phase-current feedback biases are injected into either an AC induction motor or a permanent-magnet synchronous motor while both motors operate. PCC features are processed by a multihead convolutional neural network and bidirectional gated recurrent unit (CNN--Bi-GRU), with raw and temporal-difference inputs and rebalanced task losses. An accuracy of 93.46\% and attack recall of 95.32\% are obtained; the attacked motor is identified correctly in every attack window when evaluated conditional on attack. Real-time window processing is supported by a mean CPU processing time of 4.50~ms. The results demonstrate FDIA detection and source identification from aggregate PCC measurements, supporting wider grid-edge monitoring with lower-cost instrumentation.

In our setup, EMUs (smart-plug form factor) are deployed at the point of common coupling (PCC) of a cyber-physical motor-drive testbed to emulate edge deployment conditions. The EMUs capture alternating-current (AC) power measurements with built-in IoT connectivity, enabling real-time window-based analysis. The hardware platform is described in a companion manuscript submitted for publication~\cite{najarEMU2026}; related smart-plug PCC measurements have also been used for battery state-of-charge estimation~\cite{najarSOC2026}. edits.old:
\subsection{Multihead Training and Validation}
The split is stratified 80/20 at seed 42: 94,157 training and 23,540 validation windows (4,626 normal; 18,914 attack). Adjacent windows share 112 of 128 samples; recordings can occur in both partitions. Validation is used for model/epoch selection, so these results do not establish independent-recording generalization.

Initial multihead training uses Adam at $10^{-3}$, up to 40 epochs, and outer task weights $(1,0.5,0.5,1,0.25,0.25)$ for attack, motor, phases, severity, start presence, and position. Fine-tuning runs 45 epochs with all six coefficients fixed at 1; task-specific class weights and masks mean gradients need not be equal. Motor loss uses attack windows; position loss uses known starts. Severity targets are divided by 0.5, with loss 0.5 active-phase MAE plus 0.5 active-phase MSE and 0.05 inactive-phase MAE. Position targets are divided by 127; start presence uses inverse-frequency binary weights.

Epoch selection averages attack balanced accuracy, conditional motor balanced accuracy, phase balanced accuracy averaged over all and attack-only windows, start-presence F1, and two regression utilities. Each regression utility is $\max(0,\min(1,1-E/(2E_{\rm ref})))$, using MAE $E$ and a training-median reference error $E_{\rm ref}$. Epoch 45 is selected; all proposed-model results use this checkpoint.
